intro: Isabelle Nef plays the Allemande from the G major suite of Élisabeth Jacquet de La Guerre’s Pièces de clavecin qui peuvent se joüer sur le viollon, published in 1707, on a 78 rpm disc from Éditions de l’Oiseau-Lyre. The first strain has eight bars and the second nine; each is played twice.

sections.label: A · First strain repeated
sections.mNote: The first strain is played a second time.

sections.label: B · Second strain, repeated
sections.mNote: The second strain is played again.

cues.title: Allemande in G major, first strain
cues.text: The allemande is in four beats to the bar and in two strains. The first strain has eight bars. It begins on an upbeat B and closes on a D major chord; bar 1 opens on a G major chord, followed by running left-hand semiquavers.
cues.evidence: Identified by comparison with the printed score; the labels, the Internet Archive record and the discographies name only an Allemande. Source: Jacquet de La Guerre, Pièces de clavecin qui peuvent se joüer sur le viollon (Paris, 1707), Suite in G major, Allemande. First edition, printed page 21 (scan of the Bibliothèque nationale de France copy, IMSLP 111449: http://conquest.imslp.info/files/imglnks/usimg/5/55/IMSLP111449-PMLP62189-Jacquet_de_La_Guerre_-_Pieces_de_Clavecin_qui_peuvent_se_jouer_sur_le_Viollon,_1707.pdf). Steve Wiberg’s edition, Due West Editions, 2009, printed page 24, whose bar numbers are used here (IMSLP 28300: http://conquest.imslp.info/files/imglnks/usimg/4/40/IMSLP28300-PMLP62189-LaGuerre_PiecesDeClavecin_1707_Complete.pdf). In the recording the pitch is about 25 cents above A = 440, so the key sounds as written. The upbeat B4 is at about 2.8 s. Bar 1 begins at about 3.3 s on a G major chord; the left hand plays G–F♯–G–A in semiquavers from about 4.4 s and B–G–C–A in quavers from about 5.7 s. In bar 8 (first ending) a D major chord, A–D–F♯ over a D bass, begins at about 37 s, and the bass runs down D–C–B–A until about 42 s. Eight bars take about 40 s, a crotchet of about 1.2 s.

cues.title: First strain repeated
cues.text: The first strain is played again from its upbeat B, at about 0:42, and closes on the same D major chord. The second ending, bar 9, leads into the second strain.
cues.evidence: Wiberg’s edition, printed page 24 (first edition, printed page 21): bar 8 is the first ending and bar 9 the second. In the recording the upbeat B4 of the repeat sounds at about 42.4 s and the G major chord of bar 1 at about 42.7 s. The D major chord of bar 8 returns at about 77.7 s, and the second strain follows at about 83.4 s.

cues.title: Éditions de l’Oiseau-Lyre
cues.text: Louise Hanson-Dyer founded Éditions de l’Oiseau-Lyre in Paris as a music press. From December 1937 it also issued 78 rpm recordings, often to accompany printed scores. This disc, O. L. 75, is dated 1942 by the Bibliothèque nationale de France; an Oiseau-Lyre discography places its release in 1938 or 1939.
cues.evidence: University of Melbourne Archives and Special Collections, “Paris Sounds 1937–1947”: the press, the first 78 rpm discs from December 1937 and the pairing of recordings with scores, https://library.unimelb.edu.au/asc/collections/rare-music/resources/paris-sounds. Date of the disc: Gallica record bpt6k127370x, https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k127370x; release in 1938 or 1939: Oiseau-Lyre discography after Jim Davidson, Lyrebird Rising (1994), p. 490, https://medieval.org/emfaq/cds/lol75.htm. Catalogue number and matrices: the disc labels in the Internet Archive item.

cues.title: Second strain, bars 10–18
cues.text: The second strain, marked Reprise, has nine bars, 10 to 18, against eight in the first. It begins on a spread D major chord. The recording plays it twice, the repeat starting at about 2:07, and ends on a G major chord at about 2:53.
cues.evidence: Wiberg’s edition, printed page 24 (first edition, printed page 21): the second strain, headed Reprise, runs from bar 10 to the first ending in bar 18; the second ending is bar 19. In the recording the D major chord of bar 10 sounds at about 83.4 s, with D in the bass and F♯ above it, and the repeat begins at about 127.5 s. Each pass takes about 44 s, or 4.9 s a bar, the same speed as the first strain. The final G major chord (G, D, B) sounds from about 173 s and is held to about 177 s.

cues.title: Titon du Tillet on her improvising, 1732
cues.text: In 1732 Titon du Tillet wrote that Jacquet de La Guerre had a marvellous talent for preluding and playing fantasias on the spot. He added that she sometimes kept a prelude and a fantasia going for half an hour.
cues.evidence: Titon du Tillet, Le Parnasse françois (Paris, 1732), entry CCXLIX, p. 636, on her improvising at the harpsichord: https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_KjX7hZEPSsgC

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The Bibliothèque nationale de France record reads “Isabelle Nef, clav.” and gives her dates as 1898–1976. The make of the instrument is not established.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Allemande of the Suite in G major in Jacquet de La Guerre’s Pièces de clavecin qui peuvent se joüer sur le viollon (Paris, 1707), EJG.06, played with both strains repeated
fields.note: The labels, the Internet Archive record, the BnF catalogue and the Oiseau-Lyre discography on medieval.org name only an Allemande and a Gigue; none names a book, suite or key, so the identification rests on comparing the recording with the printed scores. Pitch tracking of the transfer (mains hum removed; tuning 25 cents above A = 440, interquartile range 20–30 cents, the same on both sides of the disc) finds an upbeat B4 at about 2.8 s; a G major chord on bar 1 from about 3.3 s, with the left hand running G–F♯–G–A in semiquavers and then B–G–C–A in quavers; a D major chord (A, D, F♯) at about 37 s with the bass descending D–C–B–A; a spread D major chord opening the second strain at about 83.4 s; and a final G major chord at about 173 s. The first strain takes about 40 s and the second about 44 s, and each is played twice. This agrees with the Allemande of the G major suite in the 1707 book (first edition, printed page 21; Wiberg’s edition, printed page 24): four beats to the bar, an upbeat B, a first strain of eight bars closing on D major, and a second strain of nine bars (10–18) that opens on a D major chord and closes on G major; at about 5 s a bar, eight and nine bars take about 40 s and 44 s. Wiberg’s edition lists La Flamande as the first piece of the D minor suite of the 1707 book, which leaves the G major suite with the only Allemande. None of the four allemandes of the 1687 book is in G major (D minor, G minor, A minor, F major). The F major allemande (EJG.04), the only one that a transfer a whole tone sharp could turn into G major, has an upbeat C and a first strain of seven bars, against the recording’s upbeat B and eight bars; its bar 1 bass line (F–C–F–G–A–B♭) differs from the recording’s even after transposition, and the file sounds a quarter of a semitone sharp on both sides with no whole-tone offset. The earlier proposal of the F major suite could not be reproduced. The Gigue on the reverse comes from the other suite of the 1707 book, in D minor, so the two sides of the disc are from different suites; no source states the pairing.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The recording date is not stated in the sources consulted. The BnF record dates the disc 1942; an Oiseau-Lyre discography after Jim Davidson’s Lyrebird Rising (1994) gives its release as 1938 or 1939, recording site and date unknown (https://medieval.org/emfaq/cds/lol75.htm). The Internet Archive upload date of 25 October 2018 is not a session date.

fields.note: No recording venue is established by the sources.

fields.label: Label

fields.note: The item’s description names an audio engineer at George Blood, L.P., and lists the item in the Boston Public Library and George Blood collections.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Digitised at 78 rpm with four stylus sizes, flat and equalised; the engineer’s preferred version is the one offered, as a variable-bitrate MP3 derived from a 24-bit FLAC.
fields.note: The pitch of the file is about 25 cents above A = 440 (interquartile range 20–30 cents), the same on both sides of the disc, and the identified score is in G major, which sounds as written. The offset cannot be divided between the harpsichord’s tuning and the speed of the disc or its transfer; no speed correction was applied here.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Jacquet de La Guerre died in 1729. This is a term calculation, not clearance of every edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU public-domain basis for a disc dated 1942 by the Bibliothèque nationale de France (release in 1938 or 1939 according to an Oiseau-Lyre discography), under the programme’s pre-1963 recording rule.
fields.note: The BnF date is a catalogue date for the disc, not an independently verified first-publication date; an Oiseau-Lyre discography (https://medieval.org/emfaq/cds/lol75.htm, after Davidson’s Lyrebird Rising) places the release in 1938 or 1939, and the label began issuing discs in December 1937. Either date is before 1963. The Gallica record marks its own digital copy as public domain; the Internet Archive item carries no licence. US first-publication evidence and US status are not established.

composer.epithet: Parisian harpsichordist and composer who played for Louis XIV as a child and published harpsichord suites, violin sonatas, cantatas and the opera Céphale et Procris.
facts: In Paris with her father, the organist Claude Jacquet; harpsichord and singing at court from the age of five
Played for Louis XIV as a child; three or four years at Madame de Montespan’s side; left the court on her marriage in 1684
Taught and gave concerts in her apartment on the Île Saint-Louis; married to the organist Marin de La Guerre
Harpsichord suites, trio and violin sonatas, cantatas, the opera Céphale et Procris and a lost Te Deum

quote.text: Finding in me at the age of five some disposition for the harpsichord, you ordered that care be taken to bring me up in it.
quote.source: Élisabeth Jacquet to Louis XIV, dedication of Les Pièces de clavessin, Paris, 1687; our translation

composer.background:
Élisabeth Jacquet was baptised in Paris on 17 March 1665. Her father, Claude Jacquet, was organist of Saint-Louis-en-l’Île, on the island in the Seine now called the Île Saint-Louis, and Catherine Cessac describes him as an excellent teacher. All four of his children became musicians: Pierre and Nicolas as organists, Anne as an instrumentalist in the household of Mademoiselle de Guise, and Élisabeth as a harpsichordist and singer. A great-uncle, Jehan Jacquet, and an uncle, also named Claude, were makers of musical instruments.

The dedication of her first printed book, in 1687, told Louis XIV how her training began. “Finding in me at the age of five some disposition for the harpsichord,” she wrote, “you ordered that care be taken to bring me up in it.” Cessac writes that she made her debut at court at that age, playing and singing before the king, and that he protected her and gave her the means to publish. Évrard Titon du Tillet, who gave her a long entry in his Parnasse françois of 1732, wrote that she was barely fifteen when she appeared at court, that the king took great pleasure in hearing her, and that Madame de Montespan kept her three or four years at her side to entertain herself and her visitors.
